newsitem.title: USA: One clue amid debris solved Oklahoma bombing.
newsitem.headline: One clue amid debris solved Oklahoma bombing.

text.p: The government's triumphant effort to convict Timothy McVeigh of the Oklahoma City bombing began with a lucky break -- a telling clue amid tons of debris.
That first stroke of good luck came in the form of a truck axle, with an identification number etched on it.

Seconds after the blast the axle whirled high in the air like a boomerang and smashed into the hood of a car. Investigators quickly determined that it came from the Ryder rental truck that had been turned into a massive bomb.
The number led investigators to a Junction City, Kansas, rental agency, where records showed a man called Robert Kling had rented the yellow Ryder truck.
However, Robert Kling quickly proved to be a phony name.
"The trail could have died right there," said former FBI deputy director Weldon Kennedy, who headed the Oklahoma City bombing investigation.
But it didn't.

Enter Lea McGown, the owner of Junction City's Dreamland Motel. Looking at the FBI's description of Kling, drawn from the memories of workers at the truck rental agency, she recalled a man who had recently rented room 25.
He called himself Timothy McVeigh.

A search of the FBI's national crime computer showed a Timothy McVeigh arrested and jailed on April 19, 1995, for traffic and weapons violations in a county some 90 miles (144 km) away from Oklahoma City. When the FBI called the county jail, McVeigh was just minutes from being released.
He proved to be the man authorities would want for much bigger crimes.

Looking back in an interview while the jury deliberated, Kennedy said, "It could have gone the other way very easily. There's a million ways that could have happened, where there could have been a break in this link of evidence."
"But that's not what happened," he added. Kennedy has left the FBI and works at a private security firm in Memphis, Tennessee.

Evidence collected by the FBI proved strong in the government's case against McVeigh. Chemical residue on a plywood panel from the truck showed it held the bomb made of fertiliser and fuel oil; traces of fertiliser and explosives were gleaned from McVeigh's earplugs and his pants pocket.

The defence's attacks on the tactics and techniques used by the FBI's crime lab apparently failed, and the jury never saw an internal report so critical of the lab that it accused one agent of tilting his findings to meet prosecutors' needs in a different case.
Kennedy said he was reluctant to attribute the successful case to "pure luck," noting the big role of "pure hard work."
"Sometimes the breaks go the other way, and you're not so lucky," he said.
But had that been the case, Kennedy said, he likes to think McVeigh would have been captured nevertheless.
His description was transmitted around the country, and at least one tipster left McVeigh's name on an FBI telephone hotline, Kennedy said.
"Somebody somewhere would have said, 'That's Tim McVeigh,'" he said.
